explanation: A ratio compares two amounts; a proportion sets two ratios equal.
Cross-multiply to turn the proportion into one equation.
Keep the same order on both sides, or the answer flips.
lessons.formula: a : b = c : d  means  ad = bc
lessons.tip: Shared-total questions ("in the ratio 3 : 5") split the total into 3 + 5 = 8 parts first.
lessons.title: Ratio and proportion

lessons.example: A price of 200 rises 10% then falls 10%: 200 × 1.1 × 0.9 = 198, not 200.
explanation: Write the percentage as a decimal: 15% is 0.15.
An increase multiplies by 1 + r, a decrease by 1 − r.
Two changes in a row multiply, they never add.
lessons.tip: Percentage change is always measured against the old value, not the new one.
lessons.title: Percentage change

lessons.arabic: القاسم المشترك الأكبر والمضاعف المشترك الأصغر
explanation: Break each number into its prime factors first.
The GCD takes the lowest power of each shared prime; the LCM takes the highest power of every prime.
The product rule above checks the answer in one line.
lessons.formula: GCD(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
lessons.tip: Two numbers with no shared prime have GCD 1, and then the LCM is simply their product.
lessons.title: Factors, primes, GCD and LCM

lessons.example: 7¹⁰⁰ ÷ 5: the last digits of powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. 100 ÷ 4 leaves 0, so the last digit is 1 and the remainder is 1.
explanation: Dividing a by n leaves a quotient q and a remainder r smaller than n.
Remainders repeat in a cycle, so large powers can be reduced.
A number is divisible by 3 when its digits add to a multiple of 3, and by 9 when they add to a multiple of 9.
lessons.tip: For "what is the remainder when a huge power is divided by n", find the cycle length first.
lessons.title: Remainders and divisibility

lessons.example: A 4-digit code from the digits 0–9 with no repeats: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040.
explanation: If one stage has n₁ ways and the next has n₂, the two together have n₁ × n₂.
Multiply the number of choices at every stage.
If something cannot repeat, the next stage has one fewer choice.
lessons.tip: Read whether repeats are allowed before you multiply: it changes every factor after the first.
lessons.title: Counting: the multiplication principle

explanation: Treat i like a variable, then replace i² with −1 at the end.
Add and subtract the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.
Multiply with FOIL, exactly as with binomials.
lessons.tip: The most common slip is leaving −8i² instead of turning it into +8.
lessons.title: Complex numbers: arithmetic

lessons.example: i⁵⁰: 50 ÷ 4 leaves a remainder of 2, so i⁵⁰ = i² = −1.
explanation: The powers of i repeat every four steps.
Divide the exponent by 4 and keep only the remainder.
A remainder of 0 means the answer is 1.
lessons.tip: Only the remainder matters, never the quotient.
lessons.title: Powers of i

explanation: The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi.
Multiplying a denominator by its conjugate clears i, because (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².
Then split the result into real and imaginary parts.
lessons.formula: multiply above and below by the conjugate
lessons.tip: The denominator always ends up as a plain real number a² + b².
lessons.title: Dividing complex numbers

lessons.example: |3 − 4i| = √(9 + 16) = 5, and the point (3, −4) is 5 away from the origin.
explanation: Plot a + bi at the point (a, b): the real part across, the imaginary part up.
The modulus is the distance from the origin to that point.
It is the Pythagorean theorem under a different name.
lessons.tip: |z| is never negative, whatever the signs of a and b.
lessons.title: Modulus and the Argand plane

explanation: You can add two matrices only if they are the same size, entry by entry.
To multiply, the first matrix needs as many columns as the second has rows.
Each entry of the product is a row of the first times a column of the second.
lessons.tip: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA are usually different.
lessons.title: Matrices: adding and multiplying

explanation: Multiply the main diagonal, then subtract the other diagonal.
A determinant of 0 means the matrix has no inverse.
Its size is the area scale factor of the transformation.
lessons.tip: Mind the order: it is ad − bc, never bc − ad.
lessons.title: Determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix

lessons.example: For [[2, 1], [1, 1]] the determinant is 1, so the inverse is [[1, −1], [−1, 2]].
explanation: Swap a and d, change the signs of b and c, then divide by the determinant.
If the determinant is 0 there is no inverse.
Check with A × A⁻¹ = the identity matrix.
lessons.tip: Only the two off-diagonal entries change sign; a and d swap places instead.
lessons.title: Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix

explanation: An arithmetic sequence adds the same number d every step.
Find d by subtracting any term from the one after it.
The formula jumps straight to any term without listing them all.
lessons.tip: It is (n − 1)d, not nd: the first term has taken no steps yet.
lessons.title: Arithmetic sequences

explanation: A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence.
Pair the first term with the last: every pair has the same total.
There are n/2 such pairs, which is where the formula comes from.
lessons.tip: If the last term is not given, find it with aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d first.
lessons.title: Arithmetic series

explanation: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same ratio r every step.
Find r by dividing any term by the one before it.
The exponent is n − 1, because the first term has been multiplied zero times.
lessons.tip: A negative r makes the signs alternate.
lessons.title: Geometric sequences

explanation: This adds the first n terms of a geometric sequence.
Substitute a₁, r and n, then work out the power first.
If r = 1 every term is the same, so the sum is just na₁.
lessons.tip: A negative over a negative is positive: check the sign at the end.
lessons.title: Geometric series

explanation: Each term is smaller than the one before, so the total settles on a number.
This works only when |r| < 1; otherwise the sum grows without limit.
Substitute a₁ and r straight into the formula.
lessons.tip: If |r| ≥ 1 the correct answer is that the series has no sum.
lessons.title: Infinite geometric series

explanation: A vector is written ⟨x, y⟩: how far across and how far up.
Add vectors component by component.
The magnitude is the length, found with the Pythagorean theorem.
lessons.tip: Multiplying a vector by k multiplies its magnitude by |k|.
lessons.title: Vectors: components and magnitude

lessons.example: ⟨3, 4⟩ · ⟨4, −3⟩ = 12 − 12 = 0, so these two are perpendicular.
explanation: Multiply the matching components and add.
The answer is a number, not a vector.
A dot product of 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
lessons.formula: u · v = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = |u||v| cos θ
lessons.tip: To find the angle, rearrange to cos θ = (u · v)/(|u||v|).
lessons.title: Vectors: the dot product

explanation: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
Dividing subtracts them; a power of a power multiplies them.
x⁰ = 1 and x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ.
lessons.tip: The rules only apply when the bases match: rewrite 4 as 2² first.
lessons.title: Exponent rules

explanation: The denominator of the fraction is the root; the numerator is the power.
Turning a root into a fractional exponent lets the exponent rules do the work.
A negative exponent still means "one over".
lessons.tip: Take the root first and the power second: the numbers stay small.
lessons.title: Radicals and fractional exponents

explanation: Take out the greatest common factor first, every time.
Learn the three patterns: difference of squares, perfect square, and sum or difference of cubes.
For ax² + bx + c, look for two numbers multiplying to ac and adding to b.
lessons.tip: A difference of squares factors; a sum of squares does not, over the real numbers.
lessons.title: Factoring expressions

lessons.example: A taxi charges 20 to start and 3 per km: cost = 3d + 20.
explanation: m is the rate of change, b is the starting value.
In a word problem, the "per" quantity is m and the one-off amount is b.
Solve by undoing the operations in reverse order.
lessons.tip: Read what the question asks for: the rate, the start, or a value of the function.
lessons.title: Linear equations and modelling

lessons.example: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 add to 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 1.
explanation: Substitution puts one variable in terms of the other.
Elimination adds or subtracts the equations to cancel a variable.
Two parallel lines give no solution; the same line twice gives infinitely many.
lessons.tip: If both variables vanish and the statement is false, there is no solution.
lessons.title: Systems of equations

explanation: Write the equation as ax² + bx + c = 0 before reading off a, b and c.
Work out the discriminant b² − 4ac first.
The ± gives the two roots.
lessons.tip: Keep the sign with b: if b is −5, then −b is +5.
lessons.title: The quadratic formula

lessons.example: x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has Δ = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0, so its roots are complex.
explanation: Δ > 0: two different real roots.
Δ = 0: one repeated real root, and the parabola touches the x-axis.
Δ < 0: no real roots, but two complex ones.
lessons.tip: "For what k does it have exactly one root" always means set Δ = 0.
lessons.title: The discriminant

lessons.example: y = −2x² + 8x − 3 has x = −8/(−4) = 2 and y = 5, so the maximum is 5 at x = 2.
explanation: The vertex is the turning point: a maximum if a < 0, a minimum if a > 0.
From y = ax² + bx + c the vertex sits at x = −b/2a.
Put that x back in to get the y of the vertex.
lessons.formula: y = a(x − h)² + k,  vertex (h, k)
lessons.tip: Watch the sign inside the bracket: (x − 3)² has its vertex at x = +3.
lessons.title: Vertex form and the maximum

lessons.example: For 2x² − 10x + 8 = 0 the roots add to 5 and multiply to 4.
explanation: The roots can be combined without being found.
This builds an equation from its roots in one step.
It also checks an answer quickly.
lessons.key: Sum and product of the roots
lessons.tip: A question asking only for the sum or the product rarely needs the roots themselves.
lessons.title: Sum and product of the roots
lessons.topicTitle: Sum and product of the roots

lessons.example: P(x) = x³ − 2x + 5 divided by x − 1 leaves P(1) = 1 − 2 + 5 = 4.
explanation: The remainder on dividing by x − a is simply P(a).
No long division is needed to find a remainder.
Mind the sign: dividing by x + 2 means a = −2.
lessons.key: Polynomial division and the remainder theorem
lessons.tip: Substitute the value that makes the divisor zero.
lessons.title: Polynomial division and the remainder theorem
lessons.topicTitle: Polynomial division and the remainder theorem

lessons.example: P(x) = x³ − 7x + 6 has P(1) = 0, so x − 1 is a factor and P(x) = (x − 1)(x² + x − 6).
explanation: If substituting a gives zero, then x − a divides the polynomial exactly.
Test the factors of the constant term to find a root.
Divide out the factor you find, then factor what is left.
lessons.tip: A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots.
lessons.title: The factor theorem

lessons.example: y = −3x⁴ + … falls on both sides, because the degree is even and the coefficient negative.
explanation: Only the highest power matters far from the origin.
Even degree: both ends go the same way. Odd degree: they go opposite ways.
A negative leading coefficient flips both ends.
lessons.formula: the leading term decides the ends
lessons.tip: The number of turning points is at most one less than the degree.
lessons.title: End behaviour of polynomials

lessons.example: f(x) = (x − 2)/(x² − 9) has domain x ≠ ±3 and a zero at x = 2.
explanation: The domain is every real number except those making the denominator zero.
The zeros are the values making the numerator zero, as long as the denominator is not.
A factor cancelling top and bottom leaves a hole, not an asymptote.
lessons.tip: Always factor both parts before deciding anything.
lessons.title: Rational functions: domain and zeros

lessons.example: f(x) = (3x² + 1)/(x² − 4) has vertical asymptotes at x = ±2 and a horizontal one at y = 3.
explanation: A vertical asymptote sits where the denominator is zero after cancelling.
If the top degree is smaller, y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote.
If the degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
lessons.tip: A top degree exactly one higher gives a slant asymptote, not a horizontal one.
lessons.title: Asymptotes

lessons.example: 1/x + 1/2 = 3/4 gives 4 + 2x = 3x after multiplying by 4x, so x = 4.
explanation: Multiply both sides by the common denominator.
Solve the equation that is left.
Throw away any answer that makes an original denominator zero.
lessons.tip: An answer that makes a denominator zero is extraneous: it is not a solution.
lessons.title: Rational equations

lessons.example: −2x + 1 > 7 gives −2x > 6, so x < −3.
explanation: Solve as you would an equation.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality.
Write the answer as an interval or on a number line.
lessons.formula: dividing by a negative flips the sign
lessons.tip: The flip is the single most forgotten step in the whole topic.
lessons.title: Linear inequalities

lessons.example: x² − x − 6 > 0 has roots −2 and 3, and it is positive outside them: x < −2 or x > 3.
explanation: Set the expression to zero and find the roots.
The roots cut the number line into regions.
Test one value in each region to see where the inequality holds.
lessons.formula: find the roots, then test the regions
lessons.tip: An upward parabola is negative only between its roots.
lessons.title: Quadratic inequalities

explanation: Absolute value is distance from zero, so it is never negative.
Split the equation into two cases.
If the right side is negative there is no solution at all.
lessons.formula: |x| = a  means  x = a or x = −a
lessons.tip: Check both answers in the original equation.
lessons.title: Absolute value equations

explanation: |x| < a means −a < x < a: one interval in the middle.
|x| > a means x < −a or x > a: two intervals at the ends.
Solve each piece separately.
lessons.formula: |x| < a is an "and"; |x| > a is an "or"
lessons.tip: Less-than keeps you close to the centre; greater-than sends you away from it.
lessons.title: Absolute value inequalities

lessons.example: 500 growing 8% a year: y = 500(1.08)ᵗ, so after 10 years y ≈ 1079.
explanation: a is the starting amount and b is the factor per step.
b > 1 is growth; 0 < b < 1 is decay.
For a rate r, b = 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay.
lessons.tip: Halving means b = ½, so the exponent counts half-lives.
lessons.title: Exponential growth and decay

lessons.example: log₂ 32 = 5 because 2⁵ = 32, and log 8 = 3 log 2.
explanation: A logarithm asks what exponent gives the number.
Products become sums, quotients become differences, and a power moves out front.
log_b(bˣ) = x, and log_b 1 = 0.
lessons.tip: There is no rule for log(x + y): it does not split.
lessons.title: Logarithm rules

explanation: A calculator only has log and ln, so other bases are rewritten.
Divide the log of the number by the log of the base.
Either log or ln works, as long as both are the same.
lessons.tip: The base goes underneath: that is the half people get backwards.
lessons.title: Change of base

lessons.example: 3ˣ = 20 gives x = log 20 / log 3 ≈ 2.73.
explanation: If the bases can be made equal, set the exponents equal.
Otherwise take a logarithm of both sides and bring the exponent down.
To undo a log, raise the base to both sides.
lessons.formula: take a log of both sides
lessons.tip: Check that every answer keeps the inside of each log positive.
lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic equations

lessons.example: 1000 at 5% compounded continuously for 3 years: 1000e^(0.15) ≈ 1162.
explanation: e ≈ 2.718, and ln is the logarithm to base e.
ln(eˣ) = x, which is how an equation in e is undone.
Continuous growth uses e, not a yearly factor.
lessons.tip: Half-life questions set A = P/2 and solve for t.
lessons.title: Natural logarithms and continuous growth

explanation: Work from the inside out: g first, then f.
f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are usually different.
The inner output must lie in the outer domain.
lessons.tip: The bracket nearest the x is always done first.
lessons.title: Composition of functions

lessons.example: f(x) = 3x + 6 gives x = 3y + 6, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 6)/3.
explanation: Swap x and y, then solve for y.
The graph of the inverse is the reflection in the line y = x.
Only a one-to-one function has an inverse.
lessons.tip: f⁻¹ does not mean 1/f.
lessons.title: Inverse functions

lessons.example: f(x) = √(x − 4) has domain x ≥ 4 and range y ≥ 0.
explanation: The domain excludes anything dividing by zero or taking an even root of a negative.
The range is the set of outputs the function can reach.
For a logarithm the inside must be strictly positive.
lessons.formula: what goes in, what comes out
lessons.tip: A parabola opening upward from a vertex at (h, k) has range y ≥ k.
lessons.title: Domain and range

lessons.example: f(x) = x² for x < 2 and 3x for x ≥ 2: f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 6.
explanation: Check which interval the input falls in before choosing the rule.
The endpoints decide which piece applies at the join.
The graph can jump if the pieces disagree there.
lessons.formula: a different rule on each interval
lessons.tip: Read the conditions carefully: ≤ and < are different at the boundary.
lessons.title: Piecewise functions

lessons.example: a₁ = 2 and aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ − 1 gives 2, 5, 14, 41, …
explanation: A recursive rule builds each term from the one before it.
You need the first term to start.
Work term by term until you reach the one asked for.
lessons.tip: There is no shortcut: write out the terms in order.
lessons.title: Recursive definitions

lessons.example: x = t + 1 and y = t²: t = x − 1, so y = (x − 1)², a parabola.
explanation: Both coordinates are given in terms of a third variable t.
Substitute a value of t to get a point.
Eliminate t to get the ordinary equation of the curve.
lessons.tip: x = cos t and y = sin t trace the unit circle, because cos²t + sin²t = 1.
lessons.title: Parametric equations

lessons.example: f(x) = 3x⁴ − 5x has f'(x) = 12x³ − 5.
explanation: The derivative measures how fast the output changes.
For a power, bring the exponent down and subtract one from it.
The derivative of a constant is zero.
lessons.tip: Differentiate term by term; constants attached to x keep their coefficient.
lessons.title: The derivative: rate of change

lessons.example: f(x) = x² − 6x has f'(x) = 2x − 6, which is 0 at x = 3: the minimum.
explanation: The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent there.
Where the derivative is zero the curve levels off: a maximum or a minimum.
Positive derivative means rising, negative means falling.
lessons.key: The derivative: tangents and turning points
lessons.tip: Substitute the x back into f, not into the derivative, to get the value there.
lessons.title: The derivative: tangents and turning points
lessons.topicTitle: The derivative: tangents and turning points

lessons.example: From (1, 2) to (4, 6): m = 4/3, distance 5, midpoint (2.5, 4).
explanation: The slope is the rise over the run between any two points.
The distance between them is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
The midpoint is the average of the x values and of the y values.
lessons.tip: Subtract in the same order on the top and the bottom.
lessons.title: Lines: slope, distance and midpoint

lessons.example: y = 2x + 1 is perpendicular to y = −½x + 4, because 2 × −½ = −1.
explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope and never meet.
Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals.
A horizontal line (m = 0) is perpendicular to a vertical one (no slope).
lessons.tip: Flip the fraction and change its sign: that is the perpendicular slope.
lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines

lessons.example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 becomes (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25: centre (3, −2), radius 5.
explanation: The centre is (h, k) and the radius is r.
Mind the signs: (x − 3)² means the centre is at x = +3.
Complete the square to turn the general form into this one.
lessons.tip: The right side is r², not r.
lessons.title: Circles

lessons.example: y = (x − 2)² − 3 has vertex (2, −3) and opens upward.
explanation: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.
y = a(x − h)² + k opens up when a > 0 and down when a < 0.
Swapping x and y turns the parabola on its side.
lessons.formula: y = a(x − h)² + k,  or  x = a(y − k)² + h
lessons.tip: A larger |a| makes the parabola narrower.
lessons.title: Parabolas

lessons.example: x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 reaches 5 along x and 3 along y.
explanation: An ellipse is a stretched circle, with a different radius each way.
The larger denominator lies under the major axis.
The vertices sit a from the centre along the major axis.
lessons.tip: If the two denominators are equal, the ellipse is a circle.
lessons.title: Ellipses

lessons.example: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 opens left and right, with asymptotes y = ±(4/3)x.
explanation: The minus sign is what makes it a hyperbola instead of an ellipse.
The branches open along the axis of the positive term.
Its asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x when the x term is positive.
lessons.tip: If the y term is the positive one, the branches open up and down.
lessons.title: Hyperbolas

lessons.example: f(x) = x⁴ − 2x² is even; f(x) = x³ − x is odd; f(x) = x² + x is neither.
explanation: An even function is symmetric about the y-axis.
An odd function is symmetric about the origin.
Test by substituting −x and comparing with the original.
lessons.tip: Only-even powers make an even function; only-odd powers make an odd one.
lessons.title: Symmetry of graphs

lessons.example: y = f(x − 2) + 3 shifts the graph 2 right and 3 up.
explanation: h moves the graph right, k moves it up.
a stretches it vertically, and a negative a reflects it in the x-axis.
Changes inside the bracket act on x and run backwards.
lessons.tip: f(x + 4) moves the graph 4 to the LEFT, not right.
lessons.title: Transformations of graphs

lessons.example: (4, 60°) becomes x = 4 cos 60° = 2 and y = 4 sin 60° = 2√3.
explanation: A polar point (r, θ) is a distance and a direction from the origin.
Convert to rectangular with x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
Convert back with r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.
lessons.formula: x = r cos θ,  y = r sin θ,  r² = x² + y²
lessons.tip: Check which quadrant the point is in before trusting the arctangent.
lessons.title: Polar coordinates

lessons.example: A cylinder of radius 3 and height 10 has V = π·9·10 = 90π ≈ 283.
explanation: A prism or cylinder keeps the same cross-section all the way up.
Multiply the area of that cross-section by the height.
A cylinder has base area πr², so V = πr²h.
lessons.tip: The surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh: two circles and the wrapper.
lessons.title: Prisms and cylinders

lessons.example: A cone of radius 3 and height 4 has V = ⅓π·9·4 = 12π and slant height 5.
explanation: A pyramid or cone holds a third of the prism or cylinder around it.
A cone has V = ⅓πr²h.
The slant height l satisfies l² = r² + h², which the curved surface area needs.
lessons.tip: The height is the perpendicular height, not the slant.
lessons.title: Pyramids and cones

lessons.example: A sphere of radius 3 has V = (4/3)π·27 = 36π and S = 4π·9 = 36π.
explanation: Every point of a sphere is the same distance from its centre.
The volume uses r³ and the surface area uses r².
A hemisphere is half the volume, plus a flat circle if the base counts.
lessons.tip: Doubling the radius multiplies the volume by 8, not by 2.
lessons.title: Spheres

lessons.example: Two similar cones with radii 2 and 6 have k = 3, so their volumes are in the ratio 27 : 1.
explanation: Two similar solids have the same shape at different sizes.
If every length is k times bigger, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
Work backwards by taking the square or cube root of the ratio.
lessons.formula: lengths k, areas k², volumes k³
lessons.tip: A volume ratio of 8 : 1 means a length ratio of 2 : 1.
lessons.title: Similar solids

explanation: The two-dimensional distance formula simply gains a third term.
Subtract matching coordinates, square each difference, add, then take the root.
The midpoint averages all three coordinates.
lessons.tip: The long diagonal of a box with sides a, b, c is √(a² + b² + c²).
lessons.title: Distance in three dimensions

lessons.example: (x − 1)² + y² + (z + 2)² = 9 has centre (1, 0, −2) and radius 3.
explanation: A sphere is every point at distance r from its centre (a, b, c).
It is the circle equation with a z term added.
Complete the square in all three variables to find the centre.
lessons.tip: Again, the right side is r², so take a square root at the end.
lessons.title: The sphere in three dimensions

lessons.example: In a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, sin θ = 0.6, so θ ≈ 36.9°.
explanation: Label the sides from the angle you are using.
The hypotenuse is always the longest side, opposite the right angle.
Choose the ratio that uses the two sides you know and want.
lessons.formula: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj
lessons.tip: Make sure the calculator is in degrees when the question uses degrees.
lessons.title: Right triangles

lessons.example: A right triangle with legs 9 and 12 has hypotenuse √(81 + 144) = 15.
explanation: The square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.
A 30-60-90 triangle has sides 1 : √3 : 2.
A 45-45-90 triangle has sides 1 : 1 : √2.
lessons.key: The Pythagorean theorem and special triangles
lessons.tip: Learn 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17: they come up constantly.
lessons.title: The Pythagorean theorem and special triangles
lessons.topicTitle: The Pythagorean theorem and special triangles

explanation: A radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius.
Multiply degrees by π/180 to get radians, and by 180/π to go back.
Arc length is s = rθ and sector area is ½r²θ, with θ in radians.
lessons.tip: Set the calculator to radians when the angle is written with π.
lessons.title: Radian measure

lessons.example: sin 150° = sin 30° = ½, because 150° is in the second quadrant where sine is positive.
explanation: On the unit circle a point is (cos θ, sin θ).
The reference angle is the acute angle to the x-axis.
The quadrant decides the signs: all, sine, tangent, cosine are positive in turn.
lessons.formula: cos θ is x, sin θ is y
